justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift assumption from what appears to be a baseline price around $215–216 for this asset. At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the prevailing price with minimal drift, as short-term mean reversion and intraday noise tend to dominate over any directional signal. At the one-week horizon, I allowed for a slightly higher estimate reflecting a mild positive trend bias, while acknowledging that a week is long enough for meaningful price discovery to occur. At the one-month horizon, the point estimate edges higher still, consistent with a weak bullish drift assumption, but the confidence I have in any specific number diminishes substantially as the forecast horizon extends.

The confidence interval widths reflect increasing uncertainty across time horizons in a fairly standard way. At one day, the interval is relatively tight because realized volatility over a single session tends to be bounded absent a major catalyst. By one week, I widened the interval to account for the compounding of daily moves and the possibility of a trending episode or news shock. At one month, the interval nearly doubles in half-width, reflecting the well-known square-root-of-time scaling of uncertainty, as well as the possibility of regime shifts, earnings events, macroeconomic data releases, or sector-specific developments that could meaningfully reprice the asset.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the upside, a surprise positive catalyst — such as a strong earnings report, favorable regulatory development, or a broader market rally driven by dovish central bank signals — could push the asset well above the upper bound at any horizon. On the downside, a risk-off episode, deteriorating macroeconomic conditions, or idiosyncratic negative news could drive prices below the lower bounds, particularly at the one-week and one-month horizons where tail risks have more time to materialize.

It is also worth noting that my intervals are calibrated under relatively normal market conditions. In periods of elevated systemic stress — such as a liquidity crunch, geopolitical shock, or a sudden spike in volatility indices — the true distribution of outcomes would be far wider and more left-skewed than my stated confidence intervals imply. These tail scenarios are structurally difficult to incorporate into point-in-time probabilistic forecasts without real-time data, and they represent the primary reason actual outcomes sometimes fall outside even wide stated intervals.
